s10.slug: MONDAY, FEBRUARY 15 · 9:40 PM · DELGADO HALL — THE FRIENDS COME HOME
body: The morning of Kevin’s nineteenth, Jack gets the first text in before the airline can.

body.text: Thank you. I’m the hangover of a holiday, boarding a plane. Nineteen at 30,000 feet. It’s a metaphor; I haven’t charted for what.

body: It’s his day off, so at four he walks down the hill to the Anchor and buys a slice of olallieberry to go. Gloria finds a candle in the drawer under the register, pink and slightly bent, left over from somebody’s other birthday.
“Who’s the lucky pie?”
“Kevin. He’s nineteen today.”
“The one with the clipboard.” She pushes the candle into the foil. “Custard. Sweet clear through, and holds its shape. Tell him I said so, hon.”

At twenty to ten the black Navigator takes the red zone again with its hazards going, and Jack, in the Fishbowl door with the paper plate under foil, watches through two panes of glass as Arturo comes round to open the doors. The handkerchief is a real one, ironed. Theo’s hand comes down on the gray shoulder and stays there while the man weeps at the same curb, over the same Navigator, apparently for the same reason.
Four of them out of the car, not five.

Kevin is first through the doors, the tag still on his roller bag in his mother’s marker, CALL MA WHEN YOU LAND, and under it now in his own, *DONE. —K.* Jack holds up the plate. Kevin reads the foil, then Jack, then the Bic that comes out of the Carhartt, and says, “Disclosure: I’m not going to ask why you carry that.”
“Open flame in a common area is a violation,” Priya says from the desk, and then, reading Kevin’s face, “Five seconds.” She clicks the stopwatch.
Kevin shuts his eyes scrubbing-in tight and blows it out in three.
“What did you wish?”
“It’s HIPAA-protected.”
“You’re not a doctor.”
“I’m a covered entity in spirit.” He takes the fork. “It’s good,” he says, mouth full, surprised. “It’s very good.”
“Did it get there?” Jack says. “Your Valentine’s.”

body.text: “On the fourteenth, in the middle of Bible study. Four people saw the card.”
“She texted me one letter. *A.* It’s the note an orchestra tunes to. I’m told that isn’t an accident.”
“She hasn’t said a word about it. I’m taking that as evidence it was read twice.”
“The brothers started a group text. It’s mostly the word *respect*.”

body: Margot comes in last and drops her one black duffel in the middle of the Fishbowl carpet. “I have forty pages,” she announces. “Thirty are about Celeste. The remaining ten concern a harpist who turned out also to be a notary, for which I have no theory.” She takes the fork out of Kevin’s hand and eats a bite of his birthday. “Control group.”

Laney comes through the lobby at a quarter to ten at night in sunglasses, with four bags and a garment bag over her shoulder like a body she’s disposing of. “Kevin, happy birthday, sugar,” she says, and kisses the air a foot from his cheek, and goes past Jack to the elevator as if he were the Pepsi machine.
“She did that to a Cinnabon in Dallas,” Kevin says, to the slice. “I mean it as comfort. It doesn’t comfort me either.” He smiles, and it is a perfectly good smile, and he finishes the crust.

By ten past ten Theo has hung ten coats in the closet of 412 in the order he packed them, shoulder to shoulder, and still has the camel on, a minute longer than a coat needs to stay on a man in a heated room. He takes it off at last and hangs it last.

Then he turns with something purple and gold in his hand. “Brees threw them,” he says. “Possibly someone near Brees.” A strand of Bacchus beads, plastic, the green gone fogged where a thumb has been holding it. He doesn’t hand it over. He crosses to the nail over Jack’s footlocker where the crucifix hangs and loops the strand so it falls to either side of the corpus like a stole, steps back, looks at what he’s done, and leaves it.
“I held your seat,” he tells the closet.
“I told you not to.”
“You did. The coat had a lovely time.”
“How was it?”
“It was a parade, Costigan.” He sits on his bed and lines his shoes up, toes to the wall. “It went by.”

Jack has had Theo’s weekends since September in three acts and a credit sequence, with floor plans. This is the review. On the bedspread the iPhone lights up face-up, and lights up again, and goes dark. Theo doesn’t turn it over.
“Tell me about the films,” he says.

So Jack does. The zither wore him down by the end of the first reel and he missed it by Sunday; he watched the last road until it was empty. *Rififi* is still in its case, and he’s a film behind and means to stay there. Doug cried at the bell, and Yusuf pretended not to see. The girl at the end of the Kubrick. The tennis racket last night, and the gin. Theo takes every answer to the end, with a sock in his hand, and asks one question at a time and doesn’t once say *Picture it*.
“And the sheriff’s daughter?”
“Snow. She says Sunday.”
“I’m glad,” Theo says, and it is short.

He turns the lamp off himself. Through the blind the streetlight reaches the nail and finds the beads, purple, gold, a fogged green, hanging to either side of the cross. Wednesday the Church goes purple. The nail is early.

Tuesday is Fat Tuesday, and Youngstown observes it in lard. The RAZR takes a long time to build the picture, in strips: a white bakery box open on the Costigans’ kitchen table, powdered sugar on the oilcloth, a jelly bleeding through the paper.

body: In the afternoon he asks for the MacBook, as instructed. “You may,” Theo says from the bed, over a Hollis reader. “Wipe the trackpad.” At the top of the feed:

body: The thumbnail is a balcony on St. Charles, beads in the air, a crowd under it with its arms up, and Theo in the camel at the rail with his mouth open, shouting at a float. At the right-hand edge, cut in half by the frame and untagged, Lena is looking down at the street. Jack clicks past it without making it bigger.
“Wipe it,” Theo says, from the bed, when Jack shuts the lid. Jack wipes it, with his cuff, in a circle.

journal.title: New Orleans
journal.text: The Saints are in the Super Bowl. Friday morning Theo, Lena, Laney, Kevin and Margot left for New Orleans in a black car with the driver who took Theo to his First Communion: the game at the Broussards’, then a week, then Bacchus. Home the fifteenth. Six tickets; one had my name on it. Theo says he’ll hold my seat. I told him don’t. Sunday I’m on Doug’s futon with Yusuf. The Saints won it, 31–17. Theo called from the street so I could hear the city. Margot was fed eleven times by the Tuesday. Monday the fifteenth, Presidents’ Day, they came home: Theo, Laney, Kevin and Margot. Four out of the car. Lena stays through Ash Wednesday. Theo won’t tell it as a story. It was a parade, he says. It went by.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes. Thursday at the window table he had a list: things to say at hour four. He’d heard about Hale’s — Laney to Margot to him — and didn’t take a side. Then he asked me what you’re supposed to feel at hour four. I told him. He wrote it down. Tuesday night he drove Clare to her grandfather’s in Santa Maria to get her violin’s bridge fixed. Hour four was the drive home. He tried what I told him. He said he wanted the drive to be shorter. She fell asleep at Buellton and he drove the rest with the radio off. Thursday he told me somebody asked him to ask me to New Orleans, that he wasn’t going to, and that who asked isn’t his to say. His grandmother wants him at Tết in New Orleans East. From New Orleans East, by text, he asked me what to send Clare for Valentine’s. I said red flowers, and sign the card himself. Tết at Mary Queen of Vietnam: his grandmother called the priest from San Jose and the priest announced him. He’s promising, he’s told. He turned nineteen on a plane, and I had an Anchor slice and a candle waiting in the Fishbowl. The wish is HIPAA-protected.

s12.slug: WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 17 · 12:10 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S → 4:00 PM · THE DELGADO STEPS — ASH WEDNESDAY
body: The picture came while he slept, and by the time he’s climbing Ocean Road toward the noon Mass he has opened it so often that the RAZR has stopped dimming the screen to save him. A forehead the size of a postage stamp, blurred where she moved: a thumbprint cross in gray, dark hair swept back off it, a motel doorframe behind with its paint coming off in strips.

body.text: they gave me one. am i allowed. the makeup girl crossed herself and wiped it off for continuity

body: He sent that over the oatmeal, which is all he’ll eat until dark.

By five past twelve St. Brendan’s has a line out the doors and down the courtyard, which is what Ash Wednesday does and no other weekday can: six men from Sigma Rho in a pack with their letters on, the women’s soccer team in warm-ups with their cleats looped around their necks, and the once-a-year people along the back wall, standing as if they might be asked to leave. Peter Haddad works the door with worship aids and no hope of enough. Gus has the organ going under all of them.

Osei preaches four minutes on a Gospel that tells everyone to anoint their heads and wash their faces so no one will know they’re fasting, and then sends them up the aisle to be marked in front of God and Sigma Rho. “Yes,” he says, to the objection before anyone has made it. “I see it too. The ash is not the fast, my friends. It is only the label on the bottle. Do not mistake it for the medicine.”

The line goes up the center aisle in two files, and the choir takes it over their heads, *Parce, Domine, parce populo tuo*, spare, Lord, spare your people, slow, the way Gus likes it, so the line can’t hurry. Jack picks Osei’s file, and it still isn’t a decision. Ahead of him a Sigma Rho sophomore takes the thumb and answers *Amen* loud enough that the soccer team turns around.

Then it’s Jack. The thumb comes up gray out of the little bowl and smells of a cold fireplace, and Osei says it as he says it to everyone: “Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return.” The thumb goes down and across, grit on the skin. Osei’s eyes stay on his for the length of the sentence. Not a word more from either side of the thumb. Then the next forehead.
Becca steps up as he turns, in her buttoned coat, and says it to the side of his face, low, in the church voice, entirely sincere: “Yours is very even.”
“Thank you, Becca. Yours will be too.”
She nods at that and goes up to the thumb.

body.text: At Communion he goes up with the line, ashes and all. It’s the second time in four days, and it still surprises his knees.
body.else: At Communion he stays in the pew with the ash on his forehead, and the line goes up past his knees, half of it frat boys who have no idea he’s anybody.

body: Kevin catches him at the courtyard gate with a thumb-sized smudge, a calculator in a plastic sleeve and a pencil behind each ear. “Orgo at two,” he says. “I’ve charted my blood sugar. It’s a cliff.”
“You get two small meals. The Church says.”
“Two collations that don’t add up to a full meal. I’m saving mine for the third hour of the exam. It’s called pacing.” He heads for the science quad at a walk that wants to be a run.

body.text: Leaving, over his shoulder: “Still no answer to what I wanted instead. I’m giving up guessing for Lent.”
body.else: Leaving, over his shoulder: “Pray for my orgo. It’s a corporal work of mercy. Visiting the sick.”

body: By four the ash on the Delgado steps has gone to class and come back: every third forehead, a lot of them faint, and a girl in a bathrobe being told by a boy in a Packers hat that she’s allowed to wash it. Jack, on the third step, hasn’t.
The RAZR’s outside screen shows its row of dashes. Wednesday. The recording runs its length, *an inmate at an Ohio correctional institution*, Danny’s name jammed into the gap, and he presses one.
“Professor.” The dayroom behind him is louder than last time; somebody has a judge show on. “Got her letter.”
“She said she would. *Small. Make him work for it.*”
“She meant it.” Paper moves near the mouthpiece. “She wrote small, Professor. Like ants. Except the capitals. Top of the first page, you ready, in capitals: THE GOAT AT CARRILLO.”

body.text: “I had Carrillo from the source. Now I got an eyewitness. You’re worse in capitals.”
body.else: “What’s Carrillo? Don’t tell me. She told me. In capitals.”

body: “She sent a picture of a horse. Sorrel. Name of Clementine. It’s on my wall where Reggie has to look at it. Reggie says it looks at him.”
“What did you say?”
“I said that’s the point of a horse. And the chaplain came down the range at noon with a thumb. Seventeen guys on the tier. Reggie asked for seconds.”
“You can’t get seconds.”
“That’s what the chaplain said. Reggie says in Portsmouth you ask till somebody says no twice.” The television roars at something and falls back. “You get yours?”
“Noon Mass. It’s still on.”
“Good.” A chair scrapes. When Danny comes back he has dropped his voice, the way he does for the thing he called to ask. “You going up Sunday?”

choices.text: *Tell him the truth: you don’t go up.*
choices.key: On Ash Wednesday you told Danny the truth: you don’t go up.

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena. Holy Family Sunday, all of us — Pop too. He stood up when he saw Pop. Pop told him they wouldn’t lose. Laughed at the TV one till the guard looked over. Paddle boats: she’s not to know. Asked the table her name, like he didn’t have it. While Ma showed Pop the machines he asked me not to let Pop sit in the truck on the third. Asked Pop about the hall; says the Cruze sounds like a boat. Pop brought him coffee with cream and sugar. He drinks it black. He drank it. Epiphany Sunday, Maria’s Sunday: Pop went in again. Danny stood up. Pop told him the Browns would win, and they did — four straight. Then a letter, in capitals: IS SHE BLIND OR DID YOU LIE. Gina’s yacht got to Trumbull. Sunday, Ma’s Sunday, Gina told him her name across the table at Trumbull and described the taco picture. He said *a NUN?* He said ask her what she lost the bet for. He laughed so hard the CO came over. Ma said happy birthday early in case my card’s late. He said late’s a Costigan tradition. Candlemas he turned twenty-three. The unit let him call on a Tuesday, for his birthday, and he spent it on me. The block sang. I told him Theo asked me to New Orleans and I said no. He asked was it because of the TV one or the veil girl. I said neither. He said that’s two. Thursday his letter to Skye came in my box, in capitals, his number in the corner. She read it to me in the Saab. ‘My brother sings like a goat at a funeral.’ ‘He’ll tell you the truth even when it costs him. That’s the whole trouble with him.’ Ash Wednesday, collect: Skye’s letter came. She wrote small, like ants, except the capitals. THE GOAT AT CARRILLO. The horse is on his wall where Reggie has to look at it. The chaplain came down the range with ashes and Reggie asked for seconds. Then he asked was I going up Sunday. I told him I don’t go up. He didn’t ask why. Least you’re going, he said. Don’t stop going. That’s the whole trouble with him.

response: “I stay in the pew, Dan. I go. I just don’t go up.”
Danny doesn’t ask why. “Huh.” On the line the dayroom goes on without either of them: the television, a chair, a man calling a number down the tier.
“Least you’re going,” Danny says. Then: “Don’t stop going, Professor. That’s the whole trouble with *me*.”

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena. Holy Family Sunday, all of us — Pop too. He stood up when he saw Pop. Pop told him they wouldn’t lose. Laughed at the TV one till the guard looked over. Paddle boats: she’s not to know. Asked the table her name, like he didn’t have it. While Ma showed Pop the machines he asked me not to let Pop sit in the truck on the third. Asked Pop about the hall; says the Cruze sounds like a boat. Pop brought him coffee with cream and sugar. He drinks it black. He drank it. Epiphany Sunday, Maria’s Sunday: Pop went in again. Danny stood up. Pop told him the Browns would win, and they did — four straight. Then a letter, in capitals: IS SHE BLIND OR DID YOU LIE. Gina’s yacht got to Trumbull. Sunday, Ma’s Sunday, Gina told him her name across the table at Trumbull and described the taco picture. He said *a NUN?* He said ask her what she lost the bet for. He laughed so hard the CO came over. Ma said happy birthday early in case my card’s late. He said late’s a Costigan tradition. Candlemas he turned twenty-three. The unit let him call on a Tuesday, for his birthday, and he spent it on me. The block sang. I told him Theo asked me to New Orleans and I said no. He asked was it because of the TV one or the veil girl. I said neither. He said that’s two. Thursday his letter to Skye came in my box, in capitals, his number in the corner. She read it to me in the Saab. ‘My brother sings like a goat at a funeral.’ ‘He’ll tell you the truth even when it costs him. That’s the whole trouble with him.’ Ash Wednesday, collect: Skye’s letter came. She wrote small, like ants, except the capitals. THE GOAT AT CARRILLO. The horse is on his wall where Reggie has to look at it. The chaplain came down the range with ashes and Reggie asked for seconds. Then he asked was I going up Sunday. I told him I went up Sunday, the first time in two weeks, and why it took two. He said don’t make it three.

response: “Sunday I went up. First time in two weeks. I had a reason for staying down, Dan, and I’ll tell you the reason some day when it isn’t on a recording.”
“Two weeks.” Danny lets the number sit. “That’s a long time, for you.” Then: “Good. Don’t make it three.”
